**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 81, verses 15–29:**

﴿So I swear by the stars that recede﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations. The first: they are the stars that recede by day and when they set. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: they are the five planets, which are Saturn, Mercury, Jupiter, Mars and Venus. This was said by ʿAli.

Regarding their being singled out for mention, there are two views:

One: because they do not face the sun. This was said by Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Muzani.

The second: because they cross the Milky Way (al-Majarra, the band of light across the sky). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: that *al-khanas* refers to wild cattle. This was said by Ibn Masʿud.

The fourth: that they are gazelles. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

A fifth interpretation is possible: that they are the angels, because they recede and are not seen. In this case, this is an independent oath. The *la* in His words ﴿So I do not swear by the stars that recede﴾ carries the three possibilities found in ﴿I do not swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾.

﴿The sweeping, hidden ones﴾. Concerning this there are five interpretations. The first: they are the stars. This was said by al-Hasan. They were called "the sweeping, hidden ones" because they run in their course.

The second: they are the five planets. This is the view of ʿAli.

*Al-kunnas* means "the concealed," derived from *al-kināS*, which is the thicket of wild animals in which they hide. Aws ibn Hajar said:

Have you not seen that God sent down His rain-cloud,
and the fawns of the gazelles in their thicket shelter?

The third: they are wild cattle, because they hide in their thickets. This was said by Ibn Masʿud.

The fourth: they are gazelles. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

The fifth: they are the angels.

﴿And by the night when it darkens﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: when it grows dark. This was said by Ibn Masʿud and Mujahid. A poet said:

Until, when their night had begun to darken,
they rode out from the edge of darkness in the pitch black.

The second: when it turns away (recedes). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd. A poet said:

Until, when the dawn breathed upon her,
and her night withdrew from her and darkened (receded).

The third: when it approaches. This was said by Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah. Its root is *al-ʿass*, which means fullness. From this, a large cup is called *ʿass* because of its fullness with what it contains. So the word is applied to the approach of night at the beginning of its fullness, and it is applied to its darkness at the completion of its fullness.

﴿And by the dawn when it breathes﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

The first: the rising of the dawn. This was said by ʿAli and Qatadah.

The second: the rising of the sun. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Concerning *tanaffasa* ("breathes") there are two views:

One: its approach became apparent.

The second: its light increased.

A third possibility is that *tanaffasa* means "lengthened," derived from the saying "the day has breathed (tanaffasa)" when it has become long.

﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾. This is the answer to the oath, meaning the Qur'an.

Concerning "the noble messenger" there are two views:

One: Gabriel. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

The second: the Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn ʿIsa. If the intended meaning is Gabriel, then its meaning is "the word of a noble messenger of God, from the Lord of the worlds," because the origin of the word, which is the Qur'an, is not from the messenger. Rather, the messenger in the first view is a conveyer, and in the second view is one to whom it is conveyed.

﴿Obeyed there, trustworthy﴾. This is Gabriel according to the more correct of the two views, meaning obeyed among those prophets to whom he descended, and trustworthy regarding what he brought down of the books.

﴿And your companion is not mad﴾, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon﴾. Concerning whom he saw there are two views:

One: that he saw his Lord on the clear horizon. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Masʿud.

The second: that he saw Gabriel on the clear horizon in his true form. Concerning this there are two views:

One: that he saw him with his eyes. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿA'isha.

The second: that he saw him with his heart, and did not see him with his eyes. This was said by Abu Dharr.

Concerning *al-ufuq* ("the horizon") there are two views:

One: that it is the place where the sun rises.

The second: the regions and directions of the sky. A poet said:

We have taken the horizons of the sky over you,
its moon and its rising stars are ours.

Based on this, there are three sayings: One: that he saw him at the eastern horizon of the sky. This was said by Sufyan.

The second: at the western horizon of the sky. This was related by Ibn Shajara.

The third: that he saw him toward Ajyad, which is the eastern part of Mecca. This was said by Mujahid.

﴿And he is not stingy with the unseen﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisai recited it with the letter *ẓāʾ* (as *bi-ẓanīn*, "suspected"). Concerning this there are two views:

One: Muhammad is not suspected of bringing about what has not been sent down to him. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: he is not weak in conveying it. This was said by al-Farra'.

The rest recited it with the letter *ḍād* (as *bi-ḍanīn*, "stingy"). Concerning this there are two views:

One: he is not stingy in teaching what he has been taught.

The second: he is not suspected of conveying what he was not commanded to convey.

﴿Where then are you going?﴾ Concerning this there are two views:

One: Where then do you turn away from the Book of God and His obedience? This was said by Qatadah.

The second: What path is more guiding and more rightly directed for you than the Book of God? This was related by Ibn ʿIsa.

A third possibility: Where will you go to escape His punishment and His retribution?

﴿And you do not will except that God wills, the Lord of the worlds﴾. Concerning this there are three views:

One: You do not will steadfastness upon the truth except that God wills it for you.

The second: You do not will guidance except that God wills it through His granting of success.

It was said that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that when His words ﴿for whoever among you wills to go straight﴾ were revealed, Abu Jahl said: "That is up to us; if we will, we go straight, and if we will, we do not go straight." So God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And you do not will except that God wills, the Lord of the worlds.﴾

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 81, verses 15–29:**

﴿So I swear by the stars that recede﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations. The first: they are the stars that recede by day and when they set. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: they are the five planets, which are Saturn, Mercury, Jupiter, Mars and Venus. This was said by ʿAli.

Regarding their being singled out for mention, there are two views:

One: because they do not face the sun. This was said by Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Muzani.

The second: because they cross the Milky Way (al-Majarra, the band of light across the sky). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: that *al-khanas* refers to wild cattle. This was said by Ibn Masʿud.

The fourth: that they are gazelles. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

A fifth interpretation is possible: that they are the angels, because they recede and are not seen. In this case, this is an independent oath. The *la* in His words ﴿So I do not swear by the stars that recede﴾ carries the three possibilities found in ﴿I do not swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾.

﴿The sweeping, hidden ones﴾. Concerning this there are five interpretations. The first: they are the stars. This was said by al-Hasan. They were called "the sweeping, hidden ones" because they run in their course.

The second: they are the five planets. This is the view of ʿAli.

*Al-kunnas* means "the concealed," derived from *al-kināS*, which is the thicket of wild animals in which they hide. Aws ibn Hajar said:

Have you not seen that God sent down His rain-cloud,
and the fawns of the gazelles in their thicket shelter?

The third: they are wild cattle, because they hide in their thickets. This was said by Ibn Masʿud.

The fourth: they are gazelles. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

The fifth: they are the angels.

﴿And by the night when it darkens﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: when it grows dark. This was said by Ibn Masʿud and Mujahid. A poet said:

Until, when their night had begun to darken,
they rode out from the edge of darkness in the pitch black.

The second: when it turns away (recedes). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd. A poet said:

Until, when the dawn breathed upon her,
and her night withdrew from her and darkened (receded).

The third: when it approaches. This was said by Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah. Its root is *al-ʿass*, which means fullness. From this, a large cup is called *ʿass* because of its fullness with what it contains. So the word is applied to the approach of night at the beginning of its fullness, and it is applied to its darkness at the completion of its fullness.

﴿And by the dawn when it breathes﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

The first: the rising of the dawn. This was said by ʿAli and Qatadah.

The second: the rising of the sun. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Concerning *tanaffasa* ("breathes") there are two views:

One: its approach became apparent.

The second: its light increased.

A third possibility is that *tanaffasa* means "lengthened," derived from the saying "the day has breathed (tanaffasa)" when it has become long.

﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾. This is the answer to the oath, meaning the Qur'an.

Concerning "the noble messenger" there are two views:

One: Gabriel. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

The second: the Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn ʿIsa. If the intended meaning is Gabriel, then its meaning is "the word of a noble messenger of God, from the Lord of the worlds," because the origin of the word, which is the Qur'an, is not from the messenger. Rather, the messenger in the first view is a conveyer, and in the second view is one to whom it is conveyed.

﴿Obeyed there, trustworthy﴾. This is Gabriel according to the more correct of the two views, meaning obeyed among those prophets to whom he descended, and trustworthy regarding what he brought down of the books.

﴿And your companion is not mad﴾, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon﴾. Concerning whom he saw there are two views:

One: that he saw his Lord on the clear horizon. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Masʿud.

The second: that he saw Gabriel on the clear horizon in his true form. Concerning this there are two views:

One: that he saw him with his eyes. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿA'isha.

The second: that he saw him with his heart, and did not see him with his eyes. This was said by Abu Dharr.

Concerning *al-ufuq* ("the horizon") there are two views:

One: that it is the place where the sun rises.

The second: the regions and directions of the sky. A poet said:

We have taken the horizons of the sky over you,
its moon and its rising stars are ours.

Based on this, there are three sayings: One: that he saw him at the eastern horizon of the sky. This was said by Sufyan.

The second: at the western horizon of the sky. This was related by Ibn Shajara.

The third: that he saw him toward Ajyad, which is the eastern part of Mecca. This was said by Mujahid.

﴿And he is not stingy with the unseen﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisai recited it with the letter *ẓāʾ* (as *bi-ẓanīn*, "suspected"). Concerning this there are two views:

One: Muhammad is not suspected of bringing about what has not been sent down to him. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: he is not weak in conveying it. This was said by al-Farra'.

The rest recited it with the letter *ḍād* (as *bi-ḍanīn*, "stingy"). Concerning this there are two views:

One: he is not stingy in teaching what he has been taught.

The second: he is not suspected of conveying what he was not commanded to convey.

﴿Where then are you going?﴾ Concerning this there are two views:

One: Where then do you turn away from the Book of God and His obedience? This was said by Qatadah.

The second: What path is more guiding and more rightly directed for you than the Book of God? This was related by Ibn ʿIsa.

A third possibility: Where will you go to escape His punishment and His retribution?

﴿And you do not will except that God wills, the Lord of the worlds﴾. Concerning this there are three views:

One: You do not will steadfastness upon the truth except that God wills it for you.

The second: You do not will guidance except that God wills it through His granting of success.

It was said that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that when His words ﴿for whoever among you wills to go straight﴾ were revealed, Abu Jahl said: "That is up to us; if we will, we go straight, and if we will, we do not go straight." So God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And you do not will except that God wills, the Lord of the worlds.﴾
